name: The Hard Pieces
summary: What a soulstone is, and the trade's two words for taking one — told through Sigrun, who released her own husband rather than let a stranger crack him, and has not said his name since.
body: Everything that thins gets thinner all the way down, and then stops. At the very bottom one thing refuses to go any further, and if the shape is broken open it falls out into the grass. It is about the size of an egg. It is warm.

This is a soulstone. It is not a soul — a soul is a whole person, and no person fits in a stone. What is in there is the last piece: one fact, one appetite, one habit of being, pressed down over centuries until it is very nearly a mineral. A thing that spent itself burning leaves a stone that is still, in some stubborn way, about burning. A thing that endured cold leaves a stone that endures it. One kind of creature, one kind of stone, no exceptions — except near the eastern mountain, where what the broken things leave behind is [[lore/the_hole_under_the_mountain|another matter]].

Because a soulstone cannot be forgotten, it cannot decay, and in a country where everything else is quietly going soft that makes it the most valuable substance there is. Work one into a blade or set it into armour and it lends you a little of what it remembers. It does not make you stronger. It makes you harder to argue with.
The people who take stones out of thinned shapes for a living have two words for the work, and everything worth knowing about any of them is in which word they use.

The polite word is releasing. It is not dishonest. A shape at Habit has nobody left inside; it is going to let go regardless, in fifty years or five hundred, and everything it still carries will go with it — except the stone, if somebody saves the stone. Put like that it is a mercy, and some of the people who do it have thought it through with care and concluded exactly that.
The other word is cracking. It is what the same people say to each other, over drink, when the bag is heavy and the mercy has been done nine times since breakfast.
The whole distance between those two words is one person wide. She stands at a forge, and her name is [[characters/646b922c|Sigrun]].

Sigrun is the weaponsmith. Her husband thinned. She watched it go the way [[lore/the_quiet|the last chapter]] says it goes — Bright, then Faded, then one morning there was a shape at her door wearing his hands, running the one habit of him that was left. She knew the trade. She knew what a wandering Habit shape is worth, how soon somebody with a good eye would find him on a road somewhere, and which of the two words that stranger would use about it afterwards, over drink.
So she shut the forge and went out to him herself. One blow. Hers.

His stone is set into the head of her hammer, and it has been in the striking of everything she has made since — every blade she sells has him somewhere in it. Buyers say her steel keeps its edge longer than steel should, and she lets them say it. She calls what she did releasing, and she has earned the word, and nobody in the trade uses either word carelessly where she can hear.

What she has not done, from that morning to this one, is say his name. Not at the fire. Not to the Chronicle — [[characters/ef25b1f0|Bettany]] asked once, gently, and there is no record of a second asking. Sigrun knows, better than anyone, what this country does to a name nobody says aloud. She has not said it anyway. Understand why, and you understand both words, and you are as ready as anybody ever is to pick a warm stone up out of the grass.

The rest of what comes off a broken shape — teeth, hide, bone, feathers, a knife somebody was still carrying — is junk, worth almost nothing and collected by absolutely everybody, because a pile of leavings is a story with the details still attached, and details are what go first. And somebody, somewhere, is buying every scrap of it, and has been for a long time, and has never once explained what for.
